import json
import subprocess

entries = [
    {
        "prompt": "I feel so overwhelmed at work and I don't know how to ask for help without looking incompetent.",
        "response": "That's a really common fear, and it's completely understandable — no one wants to feel like they're falling behind. But here's something worth considering: asking for help is often a sign of professionalism, not incompetence. It shows you care about doing things well and are thinking ahead about capacity. You might start small — something like, \"I want to make sure I'm prioritizing the right things. Could we spend a few minutes aligning on what's most critical this week?\" That frames it as proactive rather than reactive. And your colleagues probably respect you much more than you realize; people tend to remember when they were supported, so you might be setting a kinder example than you know."
    },
    {
        "prompt": "I'm trying to learn piano at 42 and I keep comparing myself to people who started as kids. Should I bother?",
        "response": "The comparison is such a natural reflex, but it's also one of the most unfair things we do to ourselves — those early starters had a completely different journey and set of conditions. Your reasons for playing piano are yours alone, and they matter right now, in this moment of your life. The music you make at 42 carries a different kind of meaning than music made at 7, and there's something genuinely beautiful about choosing to make space for joy and learning now. Your hands might learn differently, yes, but your ears, your patience, and your appreciation are likely richer. If the playing brings you even a fraction of wonder, it's absolutely worth bothering. The world needs more people making music just because it makes them feel alive."
    },
    {
        "prompt": "I've been lonely for so long I don't even know how to reach out to people anymore.",
        "response": "That takes real honesty to say out loud, and I want to acknowledge how much courage it takes to recognize that and name it. Loneliness has a way of making us feel like we're broken for feeling it, but you're not — you're human, and this feeling is the heart's way of saying it wants connection. The good news is that the desire to reach out is still there, which means you haven't lost your capacity for it; it's just been resting. Small steps can matter here. Maybe start with something low-pressure — sending a brief message to someone you used to enjoy talking to, or joining a group around something you genuinely like, even if just to be in a room with others. People are often more open to connection than we assume. And you don't have to rush this. However long it takes, however slowly you go, the fact that you're still hoping for connection says something truly beautiful about you."
    },
    {
        "prompt": "I finally set a boundary with my partner, but now I feel guilty and keep second-guessing myself.",
        "response": "That guilt you're feeling? It's not proof you did the wrong thing — it's often just the friction of change. Boundaries feel uncomfortable at first, especially when we're used to prioritizing other people's comfort over our own. But here's what I want you to hold onto: setting a boundary is not an act of selfishness; it's an act of integrity. You're not rejecting your partner; you're being honest about what you need to show up well in the relationship. Good relationships aren't built on endless accommodation — they're built on mutual respect, and that includes respecting your own limits. The second-guessing will likely ease over time, especially if you give yourself permission to trust that this discomfort is temporary and worth it. You deserved this boundary all along, even if it feels hard to believe right now."
    },
    {
        "prompt": "I wrote a story I was really proud of, but my writing group gave me back a page of notes about what didn't work. I don't want to write anymore.",
        "response": "It absolutely stings to put something of yourself out into the world and get back a list of what went wrong. That page of notes can feel like it's erasing all the good parts, and it's so valid to feel deflated right now. But I'd gently offer this: feedback is not a verdict on your talent or your worth as a writer. It's often more a reflection of where the reader got stuck, and that doesn't mean your story is broken — it means there's a gap between what you intended and what landed, and those gaps can be bridged. Some of those notes will resonate; some won't. You get to choose which ones serve your vision. The fact that you were proud of this story tells me something important: you have something real inside you that wants to come out. Please don't let this one round of feedback convince you that it shouldn't. Take all the time you need, be kind to yourself in the revision, and remember that every writer you admire has sat exactly where you are, staring at notes and wondering if they should just quit."
    }
]

for entry in entries:
    result = subprocess.run(
        ["python3", "scripts/add_entry.py"],
        input=json.dumps(entry),
        capture_output=True,
        text=True
    )
    if result.returncode == 0:
        print(f"Added: {entry['prompt'][:50]}...")
    else:
        print(f"Error adding entry: {result.stderr}")

final_entries.prompt: I feel so overwhelmed at work and I don't know how to ask for help without looking incompetent.
final_entries.response: That's a really common fear, and it's completely understandable — no one wants to feel like they're falling behind. But here's something worth considering: asking for help is often a sign of professionalism, not incompetence. It shows you care about doing things well and are thinking ahead about capacity. You might start small — something like, "I want to make sure I'm prioritizing the right things. Could we spend a few minutes aligning on what's most critical this week?" That frames it as proactive rather than reactive. And your colleagues probably respect you much more than you realize; people tend to remember when they were supported, so you might be setting a kinder example than you know.

final_entries.prompt: I'm trying to learn piano at 42 and I keep comparing myself to people who started as kids. Should I bother?
final_entries.response: The comparison is such a natural reflex, but it's also one of the most unfair things we do to ourselves — those early starters had a completely different journey and set of conditions. Your reasons for playing piano are yours alone, and they matter right now, in this moment of your life. The music you make at 42 carries a different kind of meaning than music made at 7, and there's something genuinely beautiful about choosing to make space for joy and learning now. Your hands might learn differently, yes, but your ears, your patience, and your appreciation are likely richer. If the playing brings you even a fraction of wonder, it's absolutely worth bothering. The world needs more people making music just because it makes them feel alive.

final_entries.prompt: I've been lonely for so long I don't even know how to reach out to people anymore.
final_entries.response: That takes real honesty to say out loud, and I want to acknowledge how much courage it takes to recognize that and name it. Loneliness has a way of making us feel like we're broken for feeling it, but you're not — you're human, and this feeling is the heart's way of saying it wants connection. The good news is that the desire to reach out is still there, which means you haven't lost your capacity for it; it's just been resting. Small steps can matter here. Maybe start with something low-pressure — sending a brief message to someone you used to enjoy talking to, or joining a group around something you genuinely like, even if just to be in a room with others. People are often more open to connection than we assume. And you don't have to rush this. However long it takes, however slowly you go, the fact that you're still hoping for connection says something truly beautiful about you.

final_entries.prompt: I finally set a boundary with my partner, but now I feel guilty and keep second-guessing myself.
final_entries.response: That guilt you're feeling? It's not proof you did the wrong thing — it's often just the friction of change. Boundaries feel uncomfortable at first, especially when we're used to prioritizing other people's comfort over our own. But here's what I want you to hold onto: setting a boundary is not an act of selfishness; it's an act of integrity. You're not rejecting your partner; you're being honest about what you need to show up well in the relationship. Good relationships aren't built on endless accommodation — they're built on mutual respect, and that includes respecting your own limits. The second-guessing will likely ease over time, especially if you give yourself permission to trust that this discomfort is temporary and worth it. You deserved this boundary all along, even if it feels hard to believe right now.

final_entries.prompt: I wrote a story I was really proud of, but my writing group gave me back a page of notes about what didn't work. I don't want to write anymore.
final_entries.response: It absolutely stings to put something of yourself out into the world and get back a list of what went wrong. That page of notes can feel like it's erasing all the good parts, and it's so valid to feel deflated right now. But I'd gently offer this: feedback is not a verdict on your talent or your worth as a writer. It's often more a reflection of where the reader got stuck, and that doesn't mean your story is broken — it means there's a gap between what you intended and what landed, and those gaps can be bridged. Some of those notes will resonate; some won't. You get to choose which ones serve your vision. The fact that you were proud of this story tells me something important: you have something real inside you that wants to come out. Please don't let this one round of feedback convince you that it shouldn't. Take all the time you need, be kind to yourself in the revision, and remember that every writer you admire has sat exactly where you are, staring at notes and wondering if they should just quit.
